notes: Ruling slot 22 = Argentine Armed Forces (Onganía's Revolución Argentina). The regime has no civilian coalition partner; slot 13 follows MD with the banned Peronist Justicialist Party, the largest movement, so it keeps starting popularity. UCR del Pueblo in 3 per MD (UCR sprite), Frondizi's MID in 2, union Peronism (62 Organizations) in 20, CGT de los Argentinos in 18, Montoneros nucleus in 5, PRT (ERP not yet founded) in 19. Aramburu's UDELPA in 0.

0.name: Unión del Pueblo Argentino
0.text:
The Union of the Argentine People is the party founded in 1963 by General Pedro Eugenio Aramburu, who led the military government that overthrew Perón in 1955. Dissolved with all parties in 1966, it survives as Aramburu's personal network of officers, politicians and businessmen, and he is quietly courted as the man for an orderly transition after Onganía.

It stands for a firmly anti-Peronist, liberal and pro-Western Argentina under strong executive authority, with elections only once order is guaranteed. Its leverage lies in Aramburu's prestige in the armed forces and among the anti-Peronist middle classes.

1.name: Partido Demócrata de Mendoza
1.text:
The Democratic Party of Mendoza is the strongest survivor of the old conservative parties of the interior, heir to the National Democrats who governed Argentina in the 1930s. Its leading figure, Francisco Gabrielli, twice governed Mendoza before 1966, and like all parties it is formally dissolved under the Revolución Argentina.

It stands for provincial autonomy, private enterprise, the interests of the wine and fruit producers and a sober, anti-Peronist republic. Pro-Western and anti-communist, its leverage lies in the Cuyo provinces, the local notables who back it and its acceptability to the military as a civilian partner.

2.name: Movimiento de Integración y Desarrollo
2.text:
The Integration and Development Movement was founded in 1963 by former president Arturo Frondizi and his adviser Rogelio Frigerio after the split of the Intransigent Radicals. It welcomed Onganía's coup in 1966, but has since drifted into opposition as the regime failed to deliver its promised modernisation.

It preaches rapid industrialisation through foreign investment, steel, oil and petrochemicals, and the integration of the Peronist masses into a national development project. Western in orientation but nationalist in economics, its leverage lies in Frondizi's intellect, Frigerio's business contacts and its bridges to both the military and Perón.

3.name: Unión Cívica Radical del Pueblo
3.text:
The People's Radical Civic Union is the main branch of Argentine Radicalism, whose president Arturo Illia was overthrown by the military in June 1966. Led by Ricardo Balbín and dissolved by decree like all parties, it keeps its committees alive informally and demands a return to constitutional government.

It stands for civil liberties, honest administration, federalism, a moderate welfare state and economic nationalism in oil and medicines. Anti-Peronist by tradition but now seeking common ground against the dictatorship, its leverage lies in the middle classes, its provincial machines and its claim to democratic legitimacy.

4.name: Partido Comunista de la Argentina
4.text:
The Communist Party of Argentina, banned and persecuted under the anti-communist laws of the Revolución Argentina, is one of the most loyal Soviet-aligned parties in the Americas. It is led by its veteran president Victorio Codovilla and general secretary Gerónimo Arnedo Álvarez, and it suffered a major Maoist split in 1968.

It calls for a democratic front against the dictatorship and the monopolies, rejects guerrilla adventurism and follows Moscow's line faithfully. Its leverage lies in disciplined cadres, cooperatives and front organisations, a foothold in some unions and the Soviet Union's interest in grain trade with Argentina.

5.name: Montoneros
5.text:
The Montoneros are a clandestine nucleus of young Catholic nationalists turned revolutionary Peronists, formed in 1968 and 1969 around Fernando Abal Medina, Carlos Gustavo Ramus and Mario Firmenich. Unknown to the public, they are training, stockpiling weapons and preparing their first spectacular action.

They see Peronism as the vehicle of Argentine socialism, demand the return of Perón and believe armed struggle is the only answer to the dictatorship. Hostile to both the oligarchy and American imperialism, their leverage lies in the radicalised Peronist and Catholic youth and in Perón's willingness to use them.

6.name: Ateneo de la República
6.text:
The Athenaeum of the Republic is a club of Catholic nationalist intellectuals, lawyers and former officials founded in 1962, which supplied many of the ministers and advisers of the Revolución Argentina. Its members inspire Onganía's paternalist vision of a community organised by corporations rather than parties.

It rejects liberal democracy, laissez-faire capitalism and Marxism alike, admires Catholic Spain and wants a hierarchical, corporatist state that would discipline both unions and big business. Distrustful of American liberalism and foreign capital, its leverage lies in its access to the presidency and the nationalist wing of the officer corps.

7.name: Secretaría de Inteligencia del Estado
7.text:
The Secretariat of State Intelligence is the presidency's intelligence service, reorganised under the Revolución Argentina and staffed largely by army officers. Since the Cordobazo of May 1969 it has expanded its surveillance of unions, universities, Peronist networks and the emerging guerrilla groups.

It regards the nation as besieged by internal subversion and treats parties, priests and journalists alike as security risks. Jealous of its autonomy, it answers to the president rather than to Washington, and its leverage lies in its files, its informers and its role in deciding who is an enemy of the state.

8.name: Los alauitas de Buenos Aires
8.text:
The Alawites of Buenos Aires are the well-established community of Syrian Alawite families who arrived early in the century and built their own charitable association, school and social club in the capital. Thoroughly Argentine yet proud of their origins, they are joined by smaller groups of Lebanese Shia in the provinces.

They cultivate a tolerant, reformist faith centred on family, education and charity, and avoid partisan politics while maintaining cordial ties with whoever governs. Their modest leverage lies in commercial success, cultural institutions and links with Syria and Lebanon.

9.name: Halqat al-Najaf
9.text:
The Najaf Circle is a small group of devout Lebanese Shia in Buenos Aires and the Tucumán region who receive sermons and treatises from the seminaries of Najaf, where the exiled Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini teaches. They pray together in private homes and remain invisible to Argentine society.

They hold that the learned clergy should govern Muslims and reject both the American and the Soviet models. They carry no weight in Argentine politics; their importance lies only in their contacts with radical clerical networks in Lebanon and Iraq.

10.name: Centro Islámico de la República Argentina
10.english: Islamic Center of the Argentine Republic
10.native_full: Centro Islámico de la República Argentina
10.text:
The Islamic Center of the Argentine Republic, founded in 1931, is the main representative body of Argentina's Sunni Muslims, most of them descendants of Syrian and Lebanese immigrants. It runs religious services, Arabic classes and charities and speaks for the community before the authorities.

Conservative and loyal to the state, it avoids politics and cultivates relations with Arab embassies, the Saudi kingdom and the Muslim World League. Its leverage is limited to a respected community of merchants, professionals and provincial notables, some of them prominent in politics as Argentines rather than as Muslims.

11.name: Halqat al-Umma
11.text:
The Umma Circle is a handful of young Palestinian and Syrian-born students in Buenos Aires who discovered the pamphlets of Hizb ut-Tahrir through relatives in Jordan and Lebanon after the defeat of 1967. They meet quietly in rented rooms and keep away from the community's established institutions.

They reject Arab nationalism, socialism and Western liberalism and call for a restored caliphate to unite the Muslim world and liberate Palestine. In Argentina they are politically insignificant, and their only leverage is the anger of a displaced generation and its links to the diaspora.

12.name: Ikhwan al-Plata
12.text:
The Brothers of the Plata are a study circle of Arab-Argentine students and young professionals in Buenos Aires who read Hasan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb and try to revive religious practice among a largely secularised second generation. They organise Qur'an lessons, Arabic courses and charity.

They seek a moral renewal of the community through education and social work, not violence, and regard the Muslim Brotherhood as a model of organisation. Far from Argentine politics, their leverage lies in community welfare and contacts with Brotherhood sympathisers in the Arab world.

13.name: Partido Justicialista
13.text:
The Justicialist Party is the political arm of the Peronist movement, the largest political force in Argentina despite being proscribed since 1955. Juan Domingo Perón directs it from exile in Madrid through his personal delegate Jorge Daniel Paladino, balancing union bosses, provincial neo-Peronists and an increasingly radical youth.

It stands for social justice, economic independence and political sovereignty: a strong state, protected industry, powerful unions and a Third Position between the blocs. Its leverage is overwhelming popular support among the working class and the conviction, shared even by its enemies, that no stable government is possible without Perón.

14.name: Partido Demócrata Cristiano
14.text:
The Christian Democratic Party was founded in 1954 by Catholic activists opposed to Perón's quarrel with the Church. Dissolved with the other parties in 1966, it is divided between a moderate wing and a leftward current around Horacio Sueldo that seeks dialogue with Peronism.

Inspired by Catholic social teaching and the Second Vatican Council, it calls for a communitarian society, worker participation, agrarian reform and a Latin American path independent of both blocs. Its base lies among Catholic professionals and students, and its leverage comes from links to the Church and to Christian democrats across the continent.

15.name: Sociedad Rural Argentina
15.text:
The Argentine Rural Society, founded in 1866, represents the great landowners and cattle breeders of the pampas, whose beef and grain exports sustain the country's balance of payments. Its exhibition at Palermo each July is attended by the president and the military commanders.

It wants low export taxes, a favourable exchange rate, secure property and the end of Peronist-style controls, and it opposes any agrarian reform. Fiercely anti-communist and pro-Western, its leverage lies in land, foreign exchange and the family ties binding the estancieros to the officer corps and the diplomatic service.

16.name: Partido Cívico Independiente
16.text:
The Independent Civic Party was founded in 1956 by Álvaro Alsogaray, the engineer and former economy minister who became Argentina's best-known champion of the free market. Alsogaray served Onganía as ambassador to Washington until 1968, while his brother Julio commanded the army until that year.

It preaches the social market economy, a stable currency, privatisation, open trade and an end to subsidies and union privileges, insisting that Argentina must 'pass the winter' of austerity. Firmly pro-American, its leverage lies in business circles, economists and liberal officers rather than in voters.

17.name: Asociación Ornitológica del Plata
17.english: Ornithological Association of the River Plate
17.text:
The Ornithological Association of the River Plate, founded in 1916, is Argentina's oldest nature conservation society, bringing together naturalists, scientists and amateur birdwatchers who publish the journal El Hornero. Its members campaign alongside the National Parks administration and provincial museums.

It calls for protecting wildlife, wetlands and the Patagonian and northern forests from hunting, drainage and uncontrolled clearing, and for expanding the network of national parks. Without a mass following or party ties, its leverage lies in scientific authority and its standing among educated urban Argentines.

18.name: CGT de los Argentinos
18.native_full: Confederación General del Trabajo de los Argentinos
18.text:
The CGT of the Argentines is the combative trade union confederation formed in March 1968 by unions that broke with the negotiators of the official CGT. Its leader Raimundo Ongaro of the printing workers is in prison, and its allies, such as Agustín Tosco of the Córdoba power workers, played a central role in the Cordobazo.

It calls for an end to the dictatorship, nationalisation of key industries, workers' control and alliance with students, priests for the Third World and the radical left. Its leverage lies in militant shop floors in Córdoba and Rosario and its moral prestige, though many unions are drifting back to the orthodox leadership.

19.name: Partido Revolucionario de los Trabajadores
19.text:
The Workers' Revolutionary Party was founded in 1965 and split in 1968 between the Trotskyist current of Nahuel Moreno and the militarist wing led by Mario Roberto Santucho, known after its newspaper El Combatiente. Santucho's party, strongest in Tucumán and Córdoba, is preparing to form its own revolutionary army.

Blending Trotskyism with Guevara's theory of armed struggle, it seeks a continental socialist revolution through prolonged people's war, rejecting both the Soviet line and Peronism. Its leverage lies in sugar workers, students and industrial militants and in its links to the Fourth International.

20.name: 62 Organizaciones Peronistas
20.text:
The 62 Organizations are the political arm of the Peronist trade unions, dominated by the metalworkers' union UOM. Their strongman Augusto Vandor was assassinated in June 1969, and the UOM is now led by Lorenzo Miguel, while the bosses bargain with the regime for the normalisation of the CGT.

They stand for Perón's return, strong unions, protected industry and wages, but also for a pragmatic union power that negotiates with any government. Hostile to Marxism and the guerrilla left, their leverage lies in union funds, the welfare schemes they control and their ability to call general strikes.

21.name: Guardia Restauradora Nacionalista
21.text:
The Nationalist Restoration Guard broke away from the Tacuara Nationalist Movement in 1960, keeping the integralist Catholic line inspired by the priest Julio Meinvielle. Small, uniformed and militant, it recruits among secondary-school and university students in Buenos Aires.

It calls for a Catholic, Hispanic and corporatist national state, rejects liberalism, Marxism and democracy, and spreads antisemitic propaganda. Its leverage lies in street violence against leftist students, in sympathisers within the police and the nationalist officer corps, and in the ideological influence of Meinvielle's writings.

22.name: Fuerzas Armadas de la República Argentina
22.native_full: Fuerzas Armadas de la República Argentina
22.text:
The Argentine Armed Forces have ruled through the Revolución Argentina since overthrowing President Illia in June 1966 and installing General Juan Carlos Onganía as president with open-ended powers. After the Cordobazo of May 1969, the army commander-in-chief, General Alejandro Agustín Lanusse, is increasingly impatient with Onganía's refusal to plan any political exit.

Guided by the doctrine of national security, the officer corps is staunchly anti-communist and anti-Peronist, aligned with the United States and determined to modernise the state. Its leverage is absolute: no government in Argentina survives without the consent of the three commanders.
22.wiki: Armed Forces of the Argentine Republic

23.name: Por Dios, Patria y Rey
23.text:
For God, Fatherland and King is the circle of Carlist émigrés, Navarrese and Basque immigrants and their Argentine sons who keep the faith of Spanish Traditionalism in Buenos Aires. They celebrate the feasts of the Carlist martyrs, read the movement's press from Pamplona and Madrid and host visiting Traditionalists.

They reject liberalism, parties and the secular republic, dreaming of a Catholic, foral and monarchical Hispanic order. They have no political following, but their ideas find an echo among Catholic nationalist intellectuals and some officers seeking an alternative to liberal democracy.
